idiom_name: no in-process lock type exists; ownership by a worker plus message passing, typed as readonly/branded data
implementation_notes: TypeScript is JavaScript with types erased at runtime: there are no concurrency primitives to express, a realm is single-threaded, and no type can require that a lock be held (the language has no linear or affine types). The only shared-memory story is SharedArrayBuffer plus Atomics, which is a flat data-oriented design rather than a per-object lock, and cross-context coordination goes through the Web Locks API's named origin-scoped locks; node:worker_threads can transfer ArrayBuffers between realms. The practical replacement is to make ownership explicit in the type system: state lives in one owner (a worker or the server) and other code interacts through messages, while Readonly, readonly arrays and branded identifiers keep local mutation out of reach.
pitfalls: No type expresses 'lock held': a branded LockId can prove a name exists, never that the caller acquired it, so any in-process lock stays a convention the compiler cannot check.
Atomics.wait cannot block the browser main thread, so a shared-memory mutex cannot be built there at all, and Node main-thread blocking stops the event loop.
SharedArrayBuffer requires cross-origin isolation headers (COOP/COEP); without them the only option left is message passing, which changes the design rather than just its implementation.
Web Locks are per-origin and cooperative: same-context code can ignore the lock, and nothing in the type system prevents calling an unprotected path.
alternative: Move the state behind an owner - a worker (worker_threads/Web Worker) addressed by messages, or the server - and use the Web Locks API only for cross-context coordination by resource name; express the ownership boundary with Readonly/branded types.
